### How to study this module

-   Redo the proofs on scratch paper: every theorem fits on one page, and it is by rewriting them that one retains the exact hypotheses.
-   Implement Laplace noise and "split" conformal yourself (a few dozen lines): the guarantees become tangible when you see the coverage histogram.
-   Whenever an $\varepsilon$ appears, ask yourself which pair of neighboring datasets it distinguishes — that is the only way to give it meaning.
-   Work through the two parts in order but in parallel in your head: chapters 6–12 replay in UQ the same moves as in privacy (guarantee, budget, utility trade-off).
-   Do the exercises on your own first (the page gives no solutions; the worked examples of each chapter are the models to follow), and compare your intervals with those of others: coverage is verified, not declared.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} The singularity of the master is to cross LLMs, graphs, and applications; now privacy and uncertainty are precisely the questions where this intersection remains the most open — DP on graphs (sensitive edges, neighbors), UQ of text and graph generations. Whether you aim for research (PhD, R&D) or data careers in a regulated sector (health, banking, insurance), knowing how to *certify* a learning system — not merely measure it — is what distinguishes an engineer trained in LLGA.
:::

## 0. Reminders: probability, concentration, DP as seen in M1 {#ch0}

Both parts of the module prove guarantees, and these proofs use a small toolbox from M1: concentration inequalities, the first definition of differential privacy, and the language of tests and intervals. This chapter lists what is assumed and where it is used.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (M1 modules)
:::

-   **Concentration inequalities** (cf. Machine Learning module, ch. 0): Markov $\mathbb{P}(Z \geq t) \leq \mathbb{E}Z/t$, Chernoff/Hoeffding for sums of Bernoullis — they provide the guarantees of the mechanisms and conformal coverage;
-   **Differential privacy, first encounter** (cf. Emerging ML module, chapter 5, if you took it; ch. 1 restates everything needed): $\varepsilon$-DP definition, Laplace noise, DP-SGD as a conclusion of federated learning — the present module takes up this basis and develops it: mechanisms (ch. 2), fine composition (ch. 3), industrial implementations (ch. 4–5);
-   **Generalization theory** (cf. Machine Learning module, ch. 8): bias-variance trade-off, error decomposition — the UQ part (ch. 6–12) answers the dual question: not just "what risk on average", but "what guarantee on *this* prediction";
-   **Training of networks** (cf. Deep Learning module, ch. 3 and 8): SGD, mini-batches, dropout — DP-SGD (ch. 4) and MC dropout (ch. 8) modify them marginally but change their nature;
-   **Statistics of tests and intervals** (cf. Refresher Statistics module, ch. 4 and 6; Machine Learning module, 4.9; Statistics in Action module, ch. 8 and 9, as an optional reference): frequentist guarantees, p-values, bootstrap — the language of the coverage guarantees of ch. 9.
::::

::: note
[Why these two parts in a single module?]{.tag} Privacy and UQ are the two faces of the "right to error" of learning systems: privacy quantifies what a model can *reveal* about the training data, UQ quantifies what it can *assert* about a new input.

Both escape evaluation by accuracy alone; both provide **formal guarantees** (inequalities, theorems) rather than empirical promises; and both converge on LLMs (ch. 11): models large enough to memorize *and* confident enough to mislead.

The thread: *make the uncertainties computable, then arbitrate them*.
:::

## 1. Differential privacy: the foundation {#ch1}

A hospital wants to publish statistics about its patients, or to train a model on their records, without revealing anything about any single patient. This chapter gives the definition that makes this promise precise and checkable.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Three mistakes recur in practice: believing that removing names and identifiers is enough, releasing statistics with no privacy budget at all, and forgetting that the privacy losses of successive releases add up (composition, ch. 3).
:::

The historical motivation (reconstructed by Dinur-Nissim, 2003): publishing "anonymized" statistics about a database is often enough to *reconstruct* the individual data by cross-referencing enough queries — naive anonymization (removing name/SSN) does not resist.

The answer of Dwork, McSherry, Nissim, Smith (2006): define protection as a property of the *mechanism* (the randomized algorithm), not of the data.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Neighboring and differential privacy]{.tag} Two databases $x, x'$ are **neighboring**, written $x \sim x'$, if they differ in the data of a single individual.

**Convention on this page** (and in these notes): one row is added or removed, unless stated otherwise. Replacing a row is a removal plus an addition, so it costs at most $2\varepsilon$ (group privacy, Proposition 1.2 with $k = 2$). On a graph, the individual is an edge (edge-DP) or a node with all its edges (node-DP): see [Advanced GNN 7.4](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch7).

A randomized mechanism $M$ is **$\varepsilon$-DP** if for every pair of neighboring databases and every subset $S$ of outputs:
$$\mathbb{P}(M(x) \in S) \;\leq\; e^{\varepsilon}\, \mathbb{P}(M(x') \in S).$$

**$(\varepsilon, \delta)$** version: the inequality may be violated with probability $\leq \delta$ (a figure to be read as "cryptographically improbable", $\delta \ll 1/n$).

Reading: changing the data of *one* person changes the distribution of the published conclusions by at most (multiplicatively) $e^\varepsilon$ — so these conclusions reveal little about that person, whatever the adversary's side knowledge.
:::

::: key
[Key result — differential privacy]{.tag}
$$\mathbb{P}(M(x) \in S) \;\leq\; e^{\varepsilon}\, \mathbb{P}(M(x') \in S) \qquad \text{for all neighbors } x \sim x' \text{ and all } S$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Three structural properties]{.tag}

1.  **Post-processing:** if $M$ is $\varepsilon$-DP, any $g \circ M$ (subsequent analysis, training, selective publication) still is — privacy does not degrade through processing of the outputs.
2.  **Group privacy:** if $x, x'$ differ on $k$ individuals,
    $$\mathbb{P}(M(x) \in S) \leq e^{k\varepsilon}\mathbb{P}(M(x') \in S).$$
3.  **Convexity:** a mixture of $\varepsilon$-DP mechanisms is $\varepsilon$-DP.

::: proof
1.  For every set $S$ of outputs,
    $$\mathbb{P}(g(M(x)) \in S) = \mathbb{P}(M(x) \in g^{-1}(S)) \leq e^\varepsilon \mathbb{P}(M(x') \in g^{-1}(S)) = e^\varepsilon \mathbb{P}(g(M(x')) \in S)$$
    — the direct image of a dominated measure preserves the Radon-Nikodym ratio.
2.  A chain of $k$ intermediate neighboring databases and multiplication of the $e^\varepsilon$.
3.  For a mixture with weights $\lambda_j$ over $M_j$ all $\varepsilon$-DP:
    $$\sum_j \lambda_j \mathbb{P}(M_j(x) \in S) \leq \sum_j \lambda_j e^\varepsilon \mathbb{P}(M_j(x') \in S) = e^\varepsilon \mathbb{P}(\text{mixture}(x') \in S).$$
    [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — Sensitivity]{.tag} The $\ell_1$ (resp. $\ell_2$) sensitivity of a query $f$ on neighboring databases:
$$\Delta_1 f = \max_{x \sim x'} \|f(x) - f(x')\|_1, \qquad \Delta_2 f = \max_{x \sim x'} \|f(x) - f(x')\|_2.$$
Computed examples:

-   counting (how many individuals satisfy $Q$?) $\Rightarrow \Delta_1 = 1$ (one row changes the count by at most 1);
-   mean over $n$ rows in $[0, 1]$ $\Rightarrow \Delta_1 = 1/n$ (adding one row shifts the mean by at most $1/n$);
-   histogram with $k$ bins $\Rightarrow \Delta_1 = 1$ (one row falls in one bin — under the add/remove convention);
-   maximum $\Rightarrow \Delta_1$ unbounded (hence the systematic clipping in practice, ch. 4).

Sensitivity measures "how much one individual can weigh" — it is what will set the noise.
:::

::: note
[Choosing $\varepsilon$ — the embarrassing question]{.tag} No universal rule, but industry benchmarks:

-   2020 US Census: a global $\varepsilon$ on the order of twenty in total for the person file (Abowd, 2018);
-   Apple (keyboard telemetry): $\varepsilon$ on the order of 4–8 per day;
-   Google (RAPPOR): $\varepsilon \approx \ln 3$ per report, cumulative budgets;
-   academic literature: $\varepsilon \leq 1$ "strict", 1–10 "reasonable".

The essential point: $\varepsilon$ is a *budget* that one spends (ch. 3), not a moral grade.
:::

## 2. Mechanisms: Laplace, Gaussian, exponential {#ch2}

The definition of chapter 1 says what a private mechanism must satisfy, not how to build one. This chapter gives the three standard constructions: add noise scaled to the sensitivity (Laplace, Gaussian), or sample a discrete answer with probabilities that depend smoothly on its quality (exponential mechanism).

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.1 — The Laplace mechanism (Dwork et al., 2006)]{.tag} Let $f$ have sensitivity $\Delta_1$. The mechanism
$$M(x) = f(x) + (Z_1, \dots, Z_k), \qquad Z_i \sim \mathrm{Laplace}\big(0, \tfrac{\Delta_1}{\varepsilon}\big)\ \text{i.i.d.}$$
is $\varepsilon$-DP. The Laplace law with parameter $b$ has density $p(z) = \frac{1}{2b} e^{-|z|/b}$.

::: proof
For an output $z \in \mathbb{R}^k$, the ratio of densities equals
$$\frac{p_x(z)}{p_{x'}(z)} = \prod_{i=1}^k \exp\!\Big( -\frac{\varepsilon}{\Delta_1}\big( |z_i - f_i(x)| - |z_i - f_i(x')| \big) \Big) = \exp\!\Big( \frac{\varepsilon}{\Delta_1} \sum_i \big( |z_i - f_i(x')| - |z_i - f_i(x)| \big) \Big).$$
By the triangle inequality,
$$\sum_i \big( |z_i - f_i(x')| - |z_i - f_i(x)| \big) \leq \sum_i |f_i(x) - f_i(x')| \leq \Delta_1,$$
hence $p_x(z)/p_{x'}(z) \leq e^{\varepsilon}$ for *all* $z$ — integrating over $S$ gives the definition (and symmetrically by exchanging $x, x'$). [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Utility, computed.** For a counting query ($\Delta_1 = 1$): $\mathbb{P}(|Z| \geq t) = e^{-\varepsilon t}$. With $\varepsilon = \ln 20 \approx 3.0$ and $b = 1/\varepsilon \approx 0.33$, the published answer is shifted

-   by at least 1 unit with probability $e^{-\varepsilon} = 5\%$,
-   by at least 3 units with probability $20^{-3} \approx 0.01\%$

— a modest noise at the scale of the single individual one seeks to mask.
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — The Gaussian mechanism, analytic form]{.tag} For $f$ with $\ell_2$ sensitivity $\Delta_2$, $M(x) = f(x) + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_k)$ is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP as soon as
$$\sigma \;\geq\; \Delta_2\, \frac{\sqrt{2 \ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon} \qquad (\varepsilon \leq 1).$$
Numerically, for $\varepsilon = 1$, $\delta = 10^{-6}$:
$$\sqrt{2\ln(1.25 \times 10^6)} = \sqrt{28.1} \approx 5.3, \qquad \text{hence } \sigma \approx 5.3\,\Delta_2 .$$

Why prefer Gaussian over Laplace in ML:

1.  Gaussian noise **composes** very well (Rényi DP, ch. 3);
2.  it is isotropic and gradient-compatible;
3.  the Gaussian tail is lighter for large $k$.

Proof: computation of the ratio of Gaussian densities bounded by $e^{\varepsilon}$ except on a set of probability $\delta$ — analysis in Dwork & Roth (2014), lemma A.1 (the factor 1.25 is a convenience constant of the upper bound).
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — The exponential mechanism (McSherry-Talwar, 2007)]{.tag} For a *non-numeric* response (choosing a median, an item, a model): a score function $u(x, h)$ (to be maximized) with sensitivity
$$\Delta_u = \max_h \max_{x \sim x'} |u(x, h) - u(x', h)|,$$
and the output law
$$\mathbb{P}(M(x) = h) \;\propto\; \exp\!\Big( \frac{\varepsilon\, u(x, h)}{2\Delta_u} \Big).$$

**Utility guarantee**: if $h^* = \arg\max_h u(x, h)$ and $u(x, h^*) - u(x, h) \geq \mathrm{GAP}$, then
$$\mathbb{P}(u(x, M(x)) \leq u(x, h^*) - \mathrm{GAP}) \leq |\mathcal H| \exp\big(-\varepsilon\, \mathrm{GAP}/(2\Delta_u)\big),$$
where $|\mathcal H|$ is the number of candidate outputs — the gap to the optimum decreases exponentially with $\varepsilon$ and the gap.

This is the mechanism of discrete choices: model selection, private top-k, auction mechanisms.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — Private median: publishing a robust statistic]{.tag} A "median age" query has unbounded sensitivity (shifting the median by one row can make it jump far if the data are concentrated). The exponential mechanism with
$$u(x, h) = -\big|\#\{i : x_i < h\} - \#\{i : x_i > h\}\big|$$
(minus the imbalance between the individuals below and above $h$; one row changes it by at most 1, so $\Delta_u = 1$) publishes an $\varepsilon$-DP median with controlled utility.

This is the canonical example of the *structural* choice of mechanism according to the query — the privacy engineer spends most of their time here, not on the noise itself.
:::

## 3. Composition: advanced and Rényi DP {#ch3}

A real analysis never releases a single statistic: it asks many queries, or, in training, takes thousands of gradient steps on the same data. This chapter computes how the privacy losses of successive mechanisms add up, and how Rényi DP keeps the total budget small.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — Basic composition, proved]{.tag} If $M_1$ is $\varepsilon_1$-DP and $M_2$, applied *after* $M_1$ and allowed to depend on its output, is $\varepsilon_2$-DP, then
$$(M_1, M_2) \text{ is } (\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\text{-DP}$$
— adaptive composition *accumulates linearly*.

::: proof
By conditioning then post-processing: for measurable $S$,
$$\mathbb{P}(M_2(M_1(x), x) \in S_2 \mid M_1(x) = m) \leq e^{\varepsilon_2} \mathbb{P}(M_2(M_1(x'), x') \in S_2 \mid M_1(x') = m)$$
— caution: conditioning only makes sense via the regular version.

The clean proof handles densities:
$$p_x(m, s) = p_x(m)\, p_x(s \mid m) \leq e^{\varepsilon_1} p_{x'}(m) \cdot e^{\varepsilon_2} p_{x'}(s \mid m) = e^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2} p_{x'}(m, s),$$
then one integrates.

Adaptivity breaks nothing because $e^{\varepsilon_2}$ bounds the ratio *for every value* of the history. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Advanced composition (Dwork, Rothblum, Vadhan, 2010)]{.tag} The composition of $k$ adaptive $(\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)$-DP mechanisms is $(\varepsilon^*, \, k\delta_0 + \delta')$-DP for every $\delta' > 0$ with
$$\varepsilon^* = \sqrt{2 k \ln(1/\delta')}\; \varepsilon_0 \;+\; k\, \varepsilon_0 \big( e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1 \big).$$
In $\sqrt k$ rather than $k$ — the idea (sketch: the proof bounds the deviation of the sum of log-ratios via Azuma, then converts a sub-Gaussian concentration into an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-type threshold).

**Numerical.** $k = 100$ releases, $\varepsilon_0 = 0.01$, $\delta' = 10^{-5}$:
$$\sqrt{200 \times 11.5} \times 0.01 = 0.48, \qquad 100 \times 0.01 \times 0.0101 = 0.010 \ \text{(second term)},$$
hence $\varepsilon^* \approx 0.49$ versus $\varepsilon = k\varepsilon_0 = 1.0$ under basic composition — twice as good. The gain explodes for large $k$ (ch. 4, DP-SGD: $k \sim 10^4$ steps).
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — Rényi DP (Mironov, 2017)]{.tag} The Rényi divergence of order $\alpha > 1$ between two laws $P, Q$:
$$D_\alpha(P \| Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1} \ln\, \mathbb{E}_{Q}\!\Big[ \Big( \frac{dP}{dQ} \Big)^{\alpha} \Big].$$
$M$ is $(\alpha, \varepsilon)$-RDP if $D_\alpha(M(x) \| M(x')) \leq \varepsilon$ for all neighboring databases. Three computational virtues:

1.  **Gaussian mechanism**: for $f$ with sensitivity $\Delta_2$, the noise $\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)$ is exactly
    $$\Big(\alpha, \frac{\alpha \Delta_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)\text{-RDP for every } \alpha;$$
2.  **composition = addition** at fixed $\alpha$: $k$ mechanisms $(\alpha, \varepsilon_i)$-RDP compose into $(\alpha, \sum_i \varepsilon_i)$-RDP.

    Proof: the joint likelihood ratio factorizes into the ratios of the successive outputs, each given the history. By the tower property, take the expectation of the last factor (raised to the power $\alpha$) conditionally on the history: $(\alpha, \varepsilon_k)$-RDP bounds it by $e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_k}$ for every history. By induction,
    $$\mathbb{E}_Q\Big[\Big(\frac{dP}{dQ}\Big)^{\alpha}\Big] \leq e^{(\alpha - 1)\sum_i \varepsilon_i},$$
    which is $D_\alpha \leq \sum_i \varepsilon_i$ — the epsilons add exactly;
3.  **conversion**:
    $$(\alpha, \varepsilon)\text{-RDP} \;\Rightarrow\; \Big(\varepsilon + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}, \delta\Big)\text{-DP}$$
    — one then optimizes $\alpha$ a posteriori.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — The RDP account, computed end to end]{.tag} 64 successive releases of the same Gaussian counting query, noise $\sigma = 8\Delta_2$, target $\delta = 10^{-6}$.

**(a) Classical route.** Each release:
$$\varepsilon_0 = \sqrt{2 \ln(1.25/\delta_0)}\,\Delta_2/\sigma \approx 5.3/8 = 0.66 .$$
Advanced composition over $k = 64$:
$$\sqrt{128 \times 13.8} \times 0.66 + 64 \times 0.66 \times (e^{0.66} - 1) \approx 27.8 + 39.5 \approx \mathbf{67}.$$
Ruinous. Here $\delta_0 = \delta' = 10^{-6}$, so the total failure probability is
$$k\delta_0 + \delta' = 64 \times 10^{-6} + 10^{-6} \approx 6.5 \times 10^{-5}.$$

**(b) RDP route.** Each release is $(\alpha, \alpha/128)$-RDP ($\alpha\Delta_2^2/2\sigma^2 = \alpha/128$); the 64 compose into $(\alpha, \alpha/2)$-RDP. Conversion:
$$\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2} + \frac{13.8}{\alpha - 1},$$
minimized at $\alpha - 1 = \sqrt{2 \times 13.8} \approx 5.3$, i.e.
$$\varepsilon^* \approx 3.13 + 2.63 \approx \mathbf{5.8}.$$

Same releases, and a total $\delta$ of $10^{-6}$ instead of $6.5 \times 10^{-5}$ — RDP accounting is better on both counts and **saves a factor of more than 10** on $\varepsilon$.

This is exactly what the "moments accountants" of DP-SGD do (ch. 4); the later improvement (amplification by subsampling, Wang et al. 2019) adds another significant factor when each step touches only a mini-batch.
:::

::: note
[The family of generalized DP]{.tag} z-CDP (Bun & Steinke, 2016 — Rényi divergence parameterized by $\rho = \varepsilon/\alpha$), f-DP (Dong, Roth, Su, 2019 — binary tests, exact frontier): same program, different representations.

The practitioner retains: *divergences with exact additivity (Rényi) give the tightest composition bounds*, and the interface (Opacus, TF Privacy, OpenDP) performs the conversion to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ for governance.
:::

## 4. Local versus global, and DP-SGD {#ch4}

Two practical questions remain: whom must the individuals trust with their raw data, and how does one train a neural network under differential privacy? This chapter answers the first with the global/local distinction and the second with DP-SGD.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Trust model: global (curator) vs local]{.tag} **Global (centralized) DP**: a trusted curator holds the raw data and randomizes the *outputs*. Better utility; single target (losing the database = catastrophe).

**Local DP**: each individual randomizes *their own data* before sending — the server never sees the truth; no third party to trust; price: much more noise (typically an extra error of order $1/\sqrt n$).

Deployment: telemetry (Apple, Google; cf. Emerging ML module ch. 3 for the link with federated learning).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Warner's randomized response (1965), the local prototype]{.tag} Sensitive question "$X \in \{0,1\}$"; the client answers the truth with probability $p$, the opposite with $1 - p$. The channel is $\varepsilon$-DP with $$e^{\varepsilon} = \frac{p}{1-p} \qquad \text{(e.g. } p = 0.75 \Leftrightarrow \varepsilon = \ln 3 \approx 1.1).$$

::: proof
Transition matrix $T = \begin{pmatrix} p & 1-p \\ 1-p & p \end{pmatrix}$. For any response $y$, the ratio
$$\frac{\mathbb{P}(y \mid X{=}1)}{\mathbb{P}(y \mid X{=}0)}$$
equals $p/(1-p)$ or $(1-p)/p$ depending on $y$, whose maximum is $p/(1-p) = e^\varepsilon$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Estimation and cost, computed.** Let $\pi$ be the true proportion and $\bar Y_n$ the proportion of 1 responses among $n$. A response is 1 with probability $r = (1-p) + (2p-1)\pi$, so debiasing gives
$$\hat\pi = \frac{\bar Y_n - (1-p)}{2p-1}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat\pi) = \frac{r(1-r)}{n\,(2p-1)^2}.$$
In the clear the variance is $\pi(1-\pi)/n$. Since
$$r - \tfrac12 = (2p-1)\big(\pi - \tfrac12\big),$$
$r$ is closer to $\tfrac12$ than $\pi$ is, so $r(1-r) \geq \pi(1-\pi)$ and the inflation factor is **at least** $(2p-1)^{-2}$:
$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\pi)}{\pi(1-\pi)/n} = \frac{r(1-r)}{\pi(1-\pi)\,(2p-1)^2} \;\geq\; \frac{1}{(2p-1)^2}.$$

At $p = 0.75$, it is 4 for $\pi = 1/2$ and about 9.3 for $\pi = 0.1$ — one needs **at least four times as many users** for the same precision as in the clear, and more for rare traits.

RAPPOR (Google Chrome): *per-bit* randomized response on a Bloom register + cohorts — the same arithmetic, at scale.
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016), summary]{.tag} At every step:

1.  draw a mini-batch $B$ by Poisson sampling, each row kept with probability $q = b/n$ ($b$ the expected batch size);
2.  **clip** each individual gradient — bounds the sensitivity at $C$:
    $$\tilde g_i = g_i / \max(1, \|g_i\|_2 / C);$$
3.  aggregate and add noise, with $\sigma$ the **noise multiplier** (the noise standard deviation is $\sigma C$):
    $$\tilde g = \frac{1}{b}\Big( \sum_{i \in B} \tilde g_i + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 C^2 I) \Big);$$
    one divides by the expected size $b$, not by the realized $|B|$, which depends on who was sampled;
4.  standard SGD step.

The final budget combines RDP composition (ch. 3) and **amplification by subsampling** — each step sees only a fraction $q$ of the individuals (Proposition 4.4 gives the simplest form). The RDP bound of a step noised with variance $\sigma^2 C^2$ is reduced by a factor of order $q^2$ (regime $q \varepsilon_{\text{step}} \lesssim 1$); exact computation in Wang, Balle, Kasiviswanathan (2019).

The "moments accountant" of Abadi et al. is the ancestor of this computation; implementations: Opacus (PyTorch), TensorFlow Privacy.

Typical settings: $\sigma \in [0.5, 1.5]$, $C$ set to the median of the gradient norms, $\varepsilon_{\text{final}} \in [1, 10]$ for modestly sized models — LLMs with 10¹¹ parameters remain an open frontier (ch. 11).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.4 — Privacy amplification by subsampling (Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, 2018)]{.tag} Let $M$ be $\varepsilon$-DP for add/remove neighbours, and run it on a Poisson subsample that keeps each row independently with probability $q$. The result is $\varepsilon'$-DP with

$$\varepsilon' = \log\big(1 + q\,(e^{\varepsilon} - 1)\big) \;\approx\; q\,(e^{\varepsilon} - 1) \quad \text{for small } q.$$

If $M$ is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP, the subsampled mechanism is $(\varepsilon', q\delta)$-DP.

::: proof
Let $x' = x \cup \{z\}$, let $T$ be the Poisson subsample of $x$, and let $P$ be the law of $M(T)$.

1.  With probability $1 - q$ the row $z$ is not sampled: the run on $x'$ also outputs $M(T)$.
2.  With probability $q$ it is: the run outputs $M(T \cup \{z\})$, of law $P_z$. Since $T \sim T \cup \{z\}$, DP gives $P_z(S) \leq e^{\varepsilon} P(S)$.
3.  Hence
    $$\mathbb{P}(M(x') \in S) = (1 - q)P(S) + qP_z(S) \leq \big(1 + q(e^{\varepsilon} - 1)\big)P(S).$$
4.  The other direction uses $P_z(S) \geq e^{-\varepsilon} P(S)$ and gives a ratio that is no larger. [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Computed.** With $\varepsilon = 1$ and $q = 0.01$,
$$\varepsilon' = \log(1.0172) \approx 0.017,$$
a gain of about sixty per step. This is what makes thousands of DP-SGD steps affordable.
::::

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from opacus import PrivacyEngine

train_ds = torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(          # toy stand-in for real data
    torch.randn(10_000, 32), torch.randint(0, 2, (10_000,)))
model = nn.Linear(32, 2)
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=256)
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)

privacy_engine = PrivacyEngine()
model, opt, loader = privacy_engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model, optimizer=opt, data_loader=loader,
    target_epsilon=3.0,          # targeted (epsilon, delta=1e-5) budget
    target_delta=1e-5, epochs=20,
    max_grad_norm=1.0,           # C: per-example clipping
)
# Ordinary training loop; at each step:
#   grad_i clipped to C, noise N(0, sigma^2 C^2), sigma set by the
#   RDP accountant + amplification by subsampling.
for epoch in range(20):
    for x, y in loader:
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(x), y)
        loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(privacy_engine.get_epsilon(delta=1e-5))   # epsilon actually spent
```

::: note
[What DP-SGD does not solve]{.tag} Utility drops with the dimension of the model (the noise is isotropic while gradients live in privileged directions); tuning $C$ is an art; rare features (a unique user!) weigh heavily after clipping; and DP protects the *data*, not the *outputs* (an incorrectly calibrated model can be private and misleading — that is the job of the UQ part).
:::

## 5. DP in industry and attacks {#ch5}

The theory of chapters 1–4 is deployed at national and planetary scale, and it is motivated by attacks that really work. This chapter describes three deployments and the two attack families that justify paying the price of a formal guarantee.

::: ex
[Example 5.1 — Three real deployments]{.tag}

**(a) 2020 US Census (Abowd, KDD 2018).** All published statistical tables go through the TopDown algorithm (optimization + Gaussian noise, exponential mechanism for the invariants); direct motivation: reconstruction attacks on the 2010 census tabulations — an internal attack exactly reconstructed a substantial fraction of the individual records (on the order of half); per-domain public ε budget, intense public debates with demographers.

**(b) Apple (2017–).** "Learning with Privacy at Scale": keyboard/emoji/QuickType telemetry in local DP (count-mean sketch + Hadamard); millions of devices, daily ε on the order of 4–8 per domain — an illustration of the "budget" that is spent every day.

**(c) Google RAPPOR (Erlingsson et al., CCS 2014).** First large academic-industry production of local DP; chain: signal (Bloom register) → permanent randomized response → instantaneous RR → cohorts; real discoveries (dominant Chrome settings).
:::

::: thm
[Landmark 5.2 — Two families of attacks that motivate the guarantees]{.tag}

**Membership inference (Shokri et al., IEEE S&P 2017).** The adversary queries the model (confidences) and classifies "was in the train?"; AUC typically well above 0.5 on rare/atypical points — the risk grows with the model's overconfidence: *calibration (ch. 7) is also a defense*.

**Unintended memorization (Carlini et al., 2019 — "The Secret Sharer").** Insert a canary ("secret key") into the train of a generator; exposure measured by the relative perplexity of the canary: LLMs memorize and *exfiltrate* verbatim sequences seen only once — a founding result for LLM privacy (ch. 11); follow-up: training extraction on GPT-2 by the same group (2021).

DP is the defense with a guarantee: an $\varepsilon$-DP mechanism bounds the membership likelihood ratio at $e^{\varepsilon}$ (hence the AUC of any adversary); the private trained model remains useful (ch. 4) provided one pays in accuracy.
:::

::: note
[Regulation]{.tag} GDPR (anonymization "reasonably impossible to re-identify"): DP is the most accepted formal reading of this criterion; sectoral frameworks (health, banking) and emerging standards (NIST, ISO/IEC 27559).

For the engineer: keep a *budget ledger* (which query, which ε spent, which composition) as one keeps an incident log — the frameworks (OpenDP, Google DP library) enforce this discipline.
:::

## 6. Uncertainty: sources and vocabulary {#ch6}

A medical classifier announces 0.97 confidence on a patient unlike any in its training set; without calibration or a coverage guarantee, the clinic cannot set the threshold below which the model should abstain. This chapter opens the second part of the module: it names the sources of such uncertainty and fixes the vocabulary of the guarantees we will prove.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty]{.tag} **Aleatoric** (data): the irreducible noise of generation — two patients identical on observed features, different outcomes; one can only *measure* it.

**Epistemic** (model): what the model ignores because it has not learned enough in that region — reducible by data; one can *reduce* it.

In heteroscedastic regression, $y = f(x) + \nu(x)\,\xi$ with standard noise $\xi$: the noise level $\nu(x)$ is aleatoric; the variance between models trained on resamples is epistemic (ch. 8 will make it operational via ensembles).

Distribution shift: a third source — the input leaves the training support; the model does not know that it does not know (ch. 9 provides a safety net; cf. [MLOps](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html#ch5) ch. 5 for drift monitoring in production).
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — The frequentist contract of calibration]{.tag} A probabilistic predictor $\hat p(y \mid x)$ is **calibrated** if among all the times it announces 80%, the truth occurs \~80% of the time:
$$\mathbb{P}\big(y = 1 \mid \hat p(x) = c\big) = c \qquad \text{for (almost) all } c \in [0, 1].$$

Calibrated ≠ accurate: always predicting the prevalence 0.3 is perfectly calibrated and useless; calibrated ≠ certain. Calibration is a *decodability* condition: without it, no threshold, cost, or action derived from the probabilities has the intended meaning.

The vocabulary of guarantees extends to sets: marginal coverage (ch. 9), conditional coverage (desired, imperfectly attainable), risk control (ch. 12).
:::

::: note
[Map of the UQ part]{.tag}

-   Ch. 7: diagnosing (calibration, Brier).
-   Ch. 8: two practical Bayesian answers (MC dropout, ensembles).
-   Ch. 9: the distribution-free guarantee par excellence (conformal).
-   Ch. 10: the "variable set size" version (quantiles).
-   Ch. 11: the transport to LLMs.
-   Ch. 12: decision-making arbitration (costs, abstention).

Philosophy of the module: UQ without a *testable guarantee* is an opinion.
:::

## 7. Calibration: diagrams, ECE, Brier {#ch7}

Before correcting a model's confidence, one must measure how wrong it is. This chapter gives the standard diagnostics — the reliability diagram, the expected calibration error and the Brier score — and the simplest fix, temperature scaling.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Reliability diagram, bins, ECE]{.tag} Partition $[0, 1]$ into $B$ bins; bin $b$ = predictions with mean confidence $\mathrm{conf}_b$, observed accuracy $\mathrm{acc}_b$, count $n_b$.

The **reliability diagram** plots $\mathrm{acc}_b$ against $\mathrm{conf}_b$ (the diagonal = perfect calibration); the **expected calibration error**:
$$\mathrm{ECE} = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \frac{n_b}{n} \big| \mathrm{acc}_b - \mathrm{conf}_b \big|.$$

Precautions on binning: the partition influences the measure (10 bins is the de facto standard); kernel / isotonic-regression variants preferable in research (Naeini et al. 2015; see also the Machine Learning module ch. 4 for evaluation curves and 4.5 for Platt and isotonic calibration).
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.2 — ECE computed by hand]{.tag} 100 binary predictions, 5 bins (mean confidences are given):

| Bin (confidence) | $n_b$ | $\mathrm{conf}_b$ | correct | $\mathrm{acc}_b$ | $\lvert \mathrm{acc}_b - \mathrm{conf}_b \rvert$ | contribution |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [0.5, 0.6) | 10 | 0.55 | 5 | 0.50 | 0.05 | 0.005 |
| [0.6, 0.7) | 20 | 0.65 | 12 | 0.60 | 0.05 | 0.010 |
| [0.7, 0.8) | 30 | 0.75 | 20 | 0.667 | 0.083 | 0.025 |
| [0.8, 0.9) | 25 | 0.85 | 18 | 0.72 | 0.13 | 0.0325 |
| [0.9, 1.0] | 15 | 0.95 | 12 | 0.80 | 0.15 | 0.0225 |

$$\mathrm{ECE} = 0.005 + 0.010 + 0.025 + 0.0325 + 0.0225 = \mathbf{0.095}.$$

Global check: total accuracy $67/100 = 67\%$, mean confidence $\sum n_b\,\mathrm{conf}_b / n = 76.5\%$ — a gap of $9.5$ points, consistent. The model is **systematically overconfident** by \~10 points, and the reliability diagram would be a curve below the diagonal bending downward.

This is the signature measured by Guo et al. (2017) on modern networks: more depth/capacity ⇒ more overconfidence, not less.
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.3 — Brier score and its decomposition (Brier 1950; Murphy 1973)]{.tag}
$$\mathrm{BS} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\hat p_i - y_i)^2, \qquad \text{decomposition:} \quad \mathrm{BS} = \underbrace{\text{reliability}}_{\text{calibration}} - \underbrace{\text{resolution}}_{\text{discrimination}} + \underbrace{\text{uncertainty}}_{\text{irreducible}}.$$

-   the reliability term (the squared, weighted ECE):
    $$\sum_b \frac{n_b}{n}(\mathrm{conf}_b - \mathrm{acc}_b)^2;$$
-   resolution measures the deviation of the $\mathrm{acc}_b$ from the prevalence;
-   uncertainty $= \bar y (1 - \bar y)$ does not depend on the model.

BS rewards *both* calibration and discrimination — it is a quadratic Brier distance; not to be confused with the log-loss (cross-entropy), which infinitely punishes wrong certainties.
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.4 — Brier computed, and the mirage of confidence]{.tag} Four predictions: $(0.9, y{=}1)$, $(0.9, y{=}1)$, $(0.9, y{=}0)$, $(0.3, y{=}1)$:
$$\mathrm{BS} = \frac{0.1^2 + 0.1^2 + 0.9^2 + 0.7^2}{4} = \frac{0.01 + 0.01 + 0.81 + 0.49}{4} = 0.33.$$
The *constant* predictor equal to the prevalence $3/4 = 0.75$ achieves
$$\mathrm{BS} = 0.75 \times 0.25 = 0.1875 < 0.33 .$$
Without information, it is better to state the base rate than to assert 90% — exactly the problem of overenthusiastic models.
:::

::: thm
[Procedure 7.5 — Temperature scaling (Guo, Pleiss, Sun, Weinberger, 2017)]{.tag} A single scalar $T > 0$ recalibrates the logits:
$$\hat p_T(y \mid x) = \mathrm{softmax}(z/T),$$
$T$ fitted by NLL on a validation set (a 1D optimization — which does not change the argmax, hence not the accuracy).

**Computed.** Two classes, logits $z = (4, 0)$:

-   $T = 1$: $\mathrm{softmax}(z) = (0.982, 0.018)$;
-   $T = 2$: $\mathrm{softmax}(2, 0) = (0.881, 0.119)$;
-   $T = 4$: $\mathrm{softmax}(1, 0) = (0.731, 0.269)$.

If the true frequency of class 1 in this neighborhood is \~75%, $T \approx 4$ is the right calibration — the ranking of the predictions is intact, only the confidence scale is corrected.

Limits: $T$ is global, calibrated on a fixed distribution; local recalibration: isotonic, Platt per bin, or conformalized calibration (ch. 9-10).
:::

```python
import numpy as np
def ece(conf, y, bins=15):
    edges = np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1); idx = np.digitize(conf, edges[1:-1])
    n = len(conf); total = 0.0
    for b in range(bins):
        m = idx == b
        if m.sum() == 0: continue
        total += (m.sum()/n) * abs(y[m].mean() - conf[m].mean())
    return total

def fit_temperature(logits, y, grid=np.linspace(0.5, 10, 200)):
    # NLL on validation, one dimension, non-parametric and sufficient for labs
    best_T, best = 1.0, np.inf
    for T in grid:
        z = logits / T
        p = np.exp(z - z.max(1, keepdims=True))
        p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
        nll = -np.log(np.clip(p[np.arange(len(y)), y], 1e-12, None)).mean()
        if nll < best: best, best_T = nll, T
    return best_T
```

## 8. Bayesian deep learning: MC dropout versus ensembles {#ch8}

Calibration corrects the confidence of one model, but a single model cannot tell what it has not learned. This chapter gives two practical ways of estimating that epistemic uncertainty — keeping dropout active at inference, and training an ensemble — and compares their costs.

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — The Bayesian framework for networks]{.tag} A prior $p(w)$ on the weights, a likelihood $p(y \mid x, w)$; the predictive integrates epistemic uncertainty:
$$p(y \mid x, \mathcal D) = \int p(y \mid x, w)\, p(w \mid \mathcal D)\, dw.$$
The posterior $p(w \mid \mathcal D)$ is intractable; the whole field is the art of approximating it without spending one's life on it (variational inference, Laplace, sampling; cf. Refresher Statistics module ch. 8 for the Bayesian foundation).
:::

::: thm
[Result 8.2 — MC dropout (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016)]{.tag} Train with dropout (Deep Learning module ch. 3) then, at inference, keep dropout active and average $S$ forward passes:
$$\hat p(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S} p(y \mid x, \hat w_s), \qquad \hat w_s \sim \text{dropout masks}.$$

Gal & Ghahramani show that this procedure is approximate variational inference (in a deep Gaussian process). The dropout masks define a Bernoulli variational distribution $q(w)$ over the weights. The dropout loss with weight decay is, up to constants and scaling, the negative ELBO, so minimizing it minimizes the gap to the posterior

$$\mathrm{KL}\big(q(w) \,\|\, p(w \mid \mathcal D)\big) = \log p(\mathcal D) - \mathrm{ELBO}(q).$$

The spirit is that of the bootstrap (Statistics in Action ch. 8): an approximate justification for a massive procedure.

**Cost:** $S$ forwards per example (typically $S \in [10, 100]$), zero retraining. **The variance between passes measures the epistemic part**.
:::

::: thm
[Result 8.3 — Deep ensembles (Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel, Blundell, 2017)]{.tag} Train $M$ independent networks (different initializations; option: adversarial training) and aggregate: average of the probabilities (classification), mixture of the predicted Gaussians (regression — the aggregated variance includes the dispersion of the means).

Bayesian position (Wilson & Izmailov, 2020): ensembles approximate the *posterior in function space* better than methods in weight space; pragmatic position: the most robust baseline of the field, at the price of $M$ trainings.
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.4 — Compared on the dimensions that matter]{.tag}

  Criterion                             MC dropout                            Deep ensembles
  ------------------------------------- ------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------
  Training cost                         1×                                    M× (typically 5)
  Inference cost                        S forwards                            M forwards
  Epistemic out of distribution         correct, sometimes underestimated     good (diversity of minima)
  Heteroscedastic aleatoric             if a variance head is added           native (mixture)
  Out-of-distribution detection (OOD)   variance of the passes → score        disagreement between members → score
  LLM scale                             dropout already exists (reasonable)   prohibitive (but cf. snapshots/weight averaging)

The famous "deep ensembles work better than one would expect from a Bayesian perspective" (a position defended by Lakshminarayanan et al.) and the counterpoint "ensembles ARE approximate Bayes model averaging" (Wilson & Izmailov): the disagreement is real.

Practice decides: *with a free training compute budget, ensembles; otherwise MC dropout*; and in all cases, evaluate the calibration (ch. 7) — not just the RMSE.
:::

::: note
[Usage warning]{.tag} These methods give uncertainties *without guarantee*: they can be silently overconfident out of distribution. Ch. 9 brings the distribution-free corrective; the typical modern combination: ensembles for diversity + conformal for the coverage guarantee.
:::

## 9. Conformal prediction: theorem and algorithm {#ch9}

Question: can we build prediction sets with coverage **guaranteed without any distributional assumption**? Answer (Vovk): yes, provided one has *exchangeable* data and accepts *marginal* coverage. This is the most useful result of the UQ part.

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Non-conformity scores and exchangeability]{.tag} Any score $s(x, y)$ (small = conforming): for classification, $s = 1 - \hat p(y \mid x)$ (softmax of the true class); for regression, $s = |y - \hat f(x)|$.

The data $Z_1, \dots, Z_n, Z_{n+1}$ are **exchangeable** if their joint law is invariant under permutation (i.i.d. ⇒ exchangeable; cf. Statistics in Action ch. 11 for the de Finetti connection — exchangeability, not i.i.d., is the true foundation).

Split conformal: split into *train* (the model learns) and *calibration* (the scores, never seen by the model).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 9.2 — Exact marginal coverage (proved)]{.tag} Let $s_1, \dots, s_n$ be the calibration scores and $s_{\text{new}}$ the score of a new pair, **exchangeable** at $(n+1)$ with continuous values.

For $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, set $k = \lceil (n+1)(1 - \alpha) \rceil$ and let $\hat q$ be the $k$-th smallest calibration score. Then
$$\mathbb{P}\big( s_{\text{new}} \leq \hat q \big) \;\geq\; 1 - \alpha \qquad \text{(exactly } k/(n+1) \text{ for continuous scores).}$$

::: proof
By exchangeability, the rank of $s_{\text{new}}$ in the multiset $\{s_1, \dots, s_n, s_{\text{new}}\}$ is **uniform over $\{1, \dots, n+1\}$**.

Justification: for every permutation $\pi$ of $\{1, \dots, n+1\}$, the law of $(Z_{\pi(1)}, \dots, Z_{\pi(n+1)})$ is that of $(Z_1, \dots, Z_{n+1})$.

The event "the rank of the last coordinate equals $r$" is the image by permutation of "the rank equals $r'$" for all $r, r'$ — same probability, and the sum of the $n+1$ probabilities equals 1: each equals $1/(n+1)$.

With continuous scores, ties are almost surely absent, and the event $\{s_{\text{new}} \leq \hat q\}$ is exactly $\{\text{rank} \leq k\}$, of probability
$$\frac{k}{n+1} \geq 1 - \alpha$$
by definition of $k$. By exchanging the roles of the $n+1$ positions, no asymptotic result is used: the guarantee is *finite-sample*.

With ties, taking $\hat q$ as the $k$-th smallest value counting strictly keeps the event
$$\{s_{\text{new}} < \hat q\} \cup \{s_{\text{new}} = \hat q\}$$
of probability $\geq k/(n+1)$ — the bound survives. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — split conformal coverage]{.tag}
$$k = \lceil (n+1)(1 - \alpha) \rceil, \qquad \hat q = s_{(k)}, \qquad \mathbb{P}\big( s_{\text{new}} \leq \hat q \big) \geq 1 - \alpha$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 9.3 — Split conformal, algorithm and worked example]{.tag} **Algorithm.**

1.  train $\hat f$ on the train set;
2.  compute the scores $s_i$ on the $n$ calibration points;
3.  $k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil$, $\hat q$ = $k$-th smallest score;
4.  predict, for a new $x$, the set $C(x) = \{y : s(x, y) \leq \hat q\}$ — in regression: $[\hat f(x) - \hat q, \hat f(x) + \hat q]$.

**Example (regression).** $n = 9$, $\alpha = 0.1$ ⇒ $k = \lceil 10 \times 0.9 \rceil = 9$. Absolute calibration residuals: 0.02 · 0.05 · 0.08 · 0.11 · 0.14 · 0.19 · 0.25 · 0.34 · 0.51 — the 9th (largest) is $\hat q = 0.51$. The prediction for any new $x$ is
$$\hat f(x) \pm 0.51, \qquad \mathbb{P}(\text{cover}) \geq 90\%$$
— *exactly* $9/10 = 90\%$ if the future residuals resemble the calibration ones.

**Classification**: same steps with $s = 1 - \hat p(\text{candidate predicted class})$; the set $C(x)$ contains the classes with sufficient softmax. Typical size 1 where the model is confident, 2-3 at the boundaries — the map of set sizes is a free ambiguity detector.

**Effect of $n$**: $\hat q$ is the empirical $(1-\alpha)$-quantile with the finite-sample correction $\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$; the $+1$ counts the new point, which is the $(n+1)$-th member of the exchangeable sample.

When $\alpha < 1/(n+1)$, $k$ exceeds $n$ (e.g. $\alpha = 0.1$, $n = 5$):
$$k = \lceil 5.4 \rceil = 6 > n ;$$
the set is then all of $\mathbb R$ — the algorithm honestly admits its ignorance.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n_tr, n_cal, n_te, alpha = 2000, 3000, 5000, 0.1
X = rng.uniform(-2, 2, size=(n_tr + n_cal + n_te, 1))
y = 2 * X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 1, len(X))              # toy i.i.d. data
X_tr, X_cal, X_te = np.split(X, [n_tr, n_tr + n_cal])   # exchangeable split
y_tr, y_cal, y_te = np.split(y, [n_tr, n_tr + n_cal])

model = LinearRegression().fit(X_tr, y_tr)              # never the calibration set
s_cal = np.abs(y_cal - model.predict(X_cal))            # non-conformity scores
k = int(np.ceil((n_cal + 1) * (1 - alpha)))             # 9 for n=9; 2701 for n=3000
qhat = np.sort(s_cal)[k - 1]
lo, hi = model.predict(X_te) - qhat, model.predict(X_te) + qhat

# empirical check of the coverage (exercise 7): it fluctuates around 0.90,
# since the guarantee holds on average over the calibration draw
cov = ((y_te >= lo) & (y_te <= hi)).mean()
print(f"qhat = {qhat:.3f}, observed coverage = {cov:.3f} (target >= {1-alpha})")
```

::: note
[What the theorem says — and does not say]{.tag} Coverage is **marginal**: on average over the draws of the calibration set *and* of new pairs.

It can be uneven across groups (conditional coverage); extensions (Mondrian conformal: per-stratum coverage; weighted conformal: known covariate shift) handle structured cases.

The train/calibration swap costs data; CV+/jackknife+ variants when $n$ is scarce. Internal link: the Statistics in Action module ch. 8 applies the same "empirical quantile + finite-sample correction" logic to bootstrap intervals.
:::

## 10. Quantile and conformalized regression {#ch10}

Split conformal regression returns intervals of the same width everywhere, even where the noise is small. This chapter makes the width adapt to the input by learning conditional quantiles, then restores the finite-sample guarantee by conformalizing them.

::: def
[Definition 10.1 — Distributional quantile, quantile regression, pinball loss (Koenker & Bassett, 1978)]{.tag} The quantile $q_\tau(x)$ of $Y \mid X = x$ satisfies $\mathbb P(Y \leq q_\tau(x) \mid x) = \tau$. One estimates it by minimizing the **pinball loss**:
$$\ell_\tau(y, \hat q) = \begin{cases} \tau\,(y - \hat q) & y \geq \hat q \\ (1 - \tau)\,(\hat q - y) & y < \hat q \end{cases} \qquad \text{(subgradients } \in [\tau - 1, \tau]\text{)}.$$

This is a convex problem (a linear program for the linear model; gradient descent for networks).

Training two heads $\hat q_{\text{lo}} = \hat q_{\alpha/2}$, $\hat q_{\text{hi}} = \hat q_{1 - \alpha/2}$ gives an *adaptive* prediction band — wide where the data are dispersed (heteroscedastic aleatoric, ch. 6). Without an exact coverage guarantee, however: the learned quantiles are optimistic on the train set.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 10.2 — Conformalized Quantile Regression (Romano, Patterson, Candès, 2019)]{.tag} Non-conformity score on calibration:
$$s_i = \max\big( \hat q_{\text{lo}}(x_i) - y_i,\; y_i - \hat q_{\text{hi}}(x_i) \big).$$
Taking $\hat q$ = the $\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$-th smallest score, the band
$$C(x) = \big[ \hat q_{\text{lo}}(x) - \hat q,\; \hat q_{\text{hi}}(x) + \hat q \big]$$
has coverage $\geq 1 - \alpha$ in finite samples (thm 9.2), *and* inherits the adaptivity of the learned quantiles: the bands vary with $x$.

In short: **CQR = quantiles (local shape) + conformal (global guarantee)** — the dominant recipe in practice.
:::

::: ex
[Example 10.3 — CQR on a synthetic case, verified]{.tag}
$$y = 2x + \sin(2x)\, (1 + 0.5x)\,\xi, \quad \xi \sim \mathcal N(0, 1) \qquad \text{(increasing variance)}.$$
In the lab:

1.  a two-head pinball network ($\tau \in \{0.05, 0.95\}$);
2.  1000 calibration points, scores $s_i$;
3.  $\hat q \approx$ corrected empirical quantile;
4.  over 100 repetitions, mean coverage 89.8% (target 90%), bands \~3× narrower than the constant-residual split conformal in calm regions — the "hourglass" plot of the bands flaring at large $x$ is the visual deliverable of the lab (exercise 8).
:::

## 11. UQ for LLMs {#ch11}

LLMs add three difficulties to the calibration problem: the output space is combinatorial (sequences, not classes); RLHF training seems to degrade verbal calibration; and generative use (a written answer) does not naturally expose token probabilities.

The M2 module [Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html) continues this part on the security and privacy side (jailbreaks ch. 5, memorization and training extraction ch. 7, membership inference and DP of LLMs ch. 8); cf. also the [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch9) module, ch. 9 (hallucination, abstention).

::: def
[Definition 11.1 — Verbalized confidence]{.tag} Ask the model for its confidence *in words*: "What's the probability that your answer is correct? Answer with a number in [0, 100]" (Lin, Hilton, Evans, 2022).

On pre-trained models (GPT-3 on trivia), verbalized confidence is *fairly well calibrated* — the model has absorbed the calibration of its pre-training log-loss.

But: Tian et al. (2023, "Just Ask for Calibration") show that aligned (RLHF) models are clearly overconfident and not very sensitive to the wording; Xiong et al. (2024) confirm the systematic overconfidence and the massive influence of the prompt (chain-of-thought, multiple choice), with calibration gaps depending on the format of several tens of ECE points.
:::

::: def
[Definition 11.2 — Three native sources of generative uncertainty]{.tag}

1.  **Token logprobs**: entropy of the distribution of the next token, or sequence probability (product); biased (length, temperature); local calibration per bin (as in ch. 7) on a labeled set.
2.  **Self-consistency**: sample $K$ trajectories (temperature > 0) and measure agreement: the frequency of the majority answer is a proxy for confidence (direct link with the ensemble diversity of ch. 8 — prediction averaging vs variance).

    Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) refine this into **semantic entropy**. Two sampled answers fall in the same cluster when a natural-language-inference (NLI) model predicts that each entails the other (*bidirectional entailment*): "Paris", "paris" and "the capital of France" are one answer for the user. With clusters $c$ and $p(c \mid x)$ the total probability of the answers in $c$,

    $$\mathrm{SE}(x) = -\sum_{c} p(c \mid x)\,\log p(c \mid x).$$

    In practice $p(c \mid x)$ is estimated by the fraction of the $K$ samples that fall in $c$ (Farquhar et al., 2024). It separates semantic uncertainty (is the answer determined?) from lexical uncertainty (how is it worded?).

    **Computed.** $K = 10$ answers form clusters of sizes 6, 3 and 1:

    $$\mathrm{SE} = -(0.6 \ln 0.6 + 0.3 \ln 0.3 + 0.1 \ln 0.1) \approx 0.90 \text{ nats}.$$

    Counting the six distinct strings as separate answers (sizes 3, 2, 1 in the first cluster, 2, 1 in the second, 1 in the third) would give about 1.70 nats: rewordings inflate the naive entropy.
3.  **Generative conformal**: apply ch. 9 to scores (negative sequence logprob, semantic conformity): response sets with guaranteed coverage — the loop is closed with distribution-free methods.

    **Conformal abstention.** Answer only when the conformal set is a single semantic cluster, and otherwise defer to a human or to retrieval (ch. 12). This is the policy of the Year 2 capstone [Y2.1](../../projects/index.html#y2-1) (GraphRAG with calibrated abstention).
:::

::: note
[The privacy wall on the LLM side]{.tag} LLMs memorize (ch. 5, Secret Sharer); DP-SGD at the scale of 10¹¹ parameters still costs too much utility for general-purpose pre-training.

Current industrial leads: DP-SGD on the alignment phases (the most sensitive data), private RAG (the data stay server-side with per-query budgets), federated learning + DP (cf. Emerging ML module ch. 3), and the systematic evaluation of extraction (canaries). An open topic — precisely the crossroads targeted by this module.
:::

## 12. Applications: deciding under uncertainty {#ch12}

A probability, an interval or a privacy budget is only useful once it drives a decision: treat or not, raise an alert, abstain and hand over to a human. This chapter turns the guarantees of the module into decision rules.

::: ex
[Example 12.1 — Medicine: calibration as a condition of care]{.tag} A risk model announcing "30% complications" triggers a costly protocol: if the patients announced at 30% actually suffer complications 45% of the time (the risk is underestimated), we undertreat; if they suffer them 15% of the time (the risk is overestimated), we overtreat — both harm patients.

Van Calster et al. (2019) document the chronic miscalibration of published clinical models and call it the "Achilles heel of predictive analytics".

Remedy: mandatory reliability diagrams (ch. 7), recalibration (temperature/isotonic), and for binary decisions: thresholds derived from utility (FN cost / FP cost), not raw probabilities.
:::

::: def
[Definition 12.2 — Expected-utility decision, abstention, risk control]{.tag} With costs $c_{\text{FP}}, c_{\text{FN}}$, the optimal classifier will predict 1 only if
$$\hat p \geq c_{\text{FP}} / (c_{\text{FP}} + c_{\text{FN}})$$
— an exact formula *if* $\hat p$ is calibrated (ch. 6). Hence the sequence of the module: calibrate (7), aggregate the sources (8-10), then decide.

**Selective abstention**: the model may answer "I don't know" when the conformal set has more than one element (or more than a budget of $m$ elements) or the CQR band is wider than a business threshold (delegation to a human); the risk-coverage curve is plotted in the lab.

**Conformal risk control** (Angelopoulos, Bates, Fisch, Lei, Schuster, 2022) chooses the threshold itself on a calibration set to control an *expectation*. Take losses $L_i(\lambda) \in [0, B]$, non-increasing in $\lambda$ (e.g. the fraction of missed findings), with empirical mean $\hat R_n(\lambda)$, and set
$$\hat\lambda = \inf\Big\{\lambda : \frac{n}{n+1}\hat R_n(\lambda) + \frac{B}{n+1} \leq \alpha\Big\}, \qquad \text{then } \mathbb{E}\big[L_{n+1}(\hat\lambda)\big] \leq \alpha.$$
With the miscoverage loss and $B = 1$, this is exactly the quantile of ch. 9.

**Learn then Test** (Angelopoulos, Bates, Candès, Jordan, Lei, 2021) gives a *high-probability* guarantee for any risk, monotone or not. It tests $H_\lambda : R(\lambda) > \alpha$ for each candidate $\lambda$ with a p-value (e.g. from Hoeffding), keeps the rejected ones under a family-wise error correction, and ensures $R(\hat\lambda) \leq \alpha$ with probability $\geq 1 - \delta$.

These are the final building blocks of the "guarantee" chain.
:::

::: ex
[Example 12.3 — Industrial assembly table]{.tag}

  Business need                             Required guarantee            Tool of the module
  ----------------------------------------- ----------------------------- -----------------------------------------
  Publish stats without re-identification   controlled ε budget           ch. 1–3 (mechanisms, RDP composition)
  Train on customer data                    formal privacy of the model   ch. 4 (DP-SGD + accountant)
  Sort alerts                               honest confidence ordering    ch. 7 (calibration, Brier)
  Per-point forecast intervals              guaranteed 90% coverage       ch. 9–10 (conformal, CQR)
  Delegate hard cases to a human            error rate of the subset      ch. 12 (selective prediction, LTT)
  LLM in production                         confidence of the answers     ch. 11 (semantic, generative conformal)

Position in the master: this module is the "guarantees" foundation of M2. The [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch9) module deepens evaluation (ch. 9), and [Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html) covers the security side.

**On graphs.** No other module of these notes treats uncertainty on graphs, so here is the transfer. MC dropout on a GNN keeps dropout active in message passing and averages $S$ passes per node; a deep ensemble trains $M$ GNNs. Split conformal for node classification calibrates on held-out labelled nodes. It stays valid in the transductive setting when calibration and test nodes form a random split and training never sees their labels (Huang, Jin, Candès, Leskovec, 2023). [Solo project 2](#projects-solo) below tests this.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Laplace mechanism.**

    a.  Re-prove thm 2.1 for $k = 1$.

    b.  Counting with ε = ln 20: probability of an error ≥ 2? ≥ 5?

    c.  50-bin histogram, total ε = 1; distribute the noise (composition) and compare the mean squared error with the vector Laplace mechanism in a single query.
2.  **★ Local DP.**

    a.  Prove the debiasing formula 4.2 and its variance factor.

    b.  In RAPPOR with 128 bits, 2 successive RRs: what ε per bit?

    c.  Sizing: precision of ±2 points on a proportion, $p = 0.75$ — how many users?
3.  **★ Calibration.**

    a.  Recompute the ECE 7.2 with 10 equal-width bins and comment on the sensitivity.

    b.  Implement the reliability diagram.

    c.  Temperature scaling on CIFAR-10 (ResNet): ECE before/after, NLL before/after, accuracy unchanged?

    d.  Show that the constant 0.75 beats the classifier of example 7.4 in both Brier score and log-loss (about 0.56 against 0.93 nats). Then replace the wrong prediction $(0.9, y{=}0)$ by $(1.0, y{=}0)$: which score stays finite, and which one punishes the wrong certainty without bound?
4.  **★★ Composition.**

    a.  Redo the computation 3.4 for $\sigma = 12$, $k = 256$, $\delta = 10^{-5}$.

    b.  Inverse: what $\sigma$ for $k = 10^4$ DP-SGD steps, ε = 2, δ = 10⁻⁵, $q = 0.01$ (approximation without amplification, then with the $q^2$ factor)?

    c.  Show that RDP composition at fixed $\alpha$ is exact for Gaussians (direct computation of the Rényi divergence of a product).
5.  **★★ DP-SGD.** On MNIST: implement per-example clipping + noise (numpy or Opacus), plot accuracy vs ε for σ ∈ {0, 0.5, 1, 2}, comment on the frontier; ablation on $C$ (0.1 to 10); verify that without clipping the mechanism is no longer DP.
6.  **★★ MC dropout versus ensembles.** 1D heteroscedastic regression: train

    a.  one network + MC dropout ($S = 50$ passes);

    b.  5 networks (deep ensemble); compare NLL, RMSE, coverage of the bands at ±2 predicted standard deviations;

    c.  test both out of distribution (extrapolation);

    d.  compare training and inference times, and conclude in a budget-constrained situation.
7.  **★★ Conformal.**

    a.  Re-prove the uniformity of the rank with ties (convention of thm 9.2).

    b.  Empirically verify the coverage over 1000 repetitions (n = 1000, α = 0.1): histogram of the coverages — what happens if the data are *not* exchangeable (drift)?

    c.  Effect of the calibration size: $n \in \{20, 100, 1000\}$;

    d.  implement per-class Mondrian and measure the coverage inequality across classes.
8.  **★★ CQR.** Reproduce example 10.3; compare the mean widths CQR vs constant split conformal; what happens if the two quantile heads cross (lo > hi)? Fix it (monotonicity constraint or sorting).
9.  **★★ Decision.** Screening: prevalence 5%, costs $c_{FP} = 1$, $c_{FN} = 20$.

    a.  Optimal threshold on calibrated probabilities.

    b.  Re-derive with probabilities overconfident by 10 points — quantify the cost of miscalibration.

    c.  Add the abstention option with a delegation cost; plot risk-coverage.
10. **★★★ LLM UQ.**

    a.  On 100 trivia questions: verbalized confidence vs actual frequency — plot the reliability diagram.

    b.  Self-consistency K = 10: correlation between agreement and correctness.

    c.  Group the answers semantically (by hand or NLI) and compare lexical vs semantic entropy.

    d.  At small scale: build a conformal set of answers and measure the coverage.
11. **★★★ Project.** Complete "privacy + UQ" pipeline: a sensitive dataset (e.g. Adult):

    1.  publish useful statistics under budget ε = 2 (mechanisms, composition);
    2.  train a private predictive model (DP-SGD);
    3.  calibrate and conformalize its outputs;
    4.  write the guarantee sheet (ε, δ, neighbour convention and accountant; coverage level and calibration-set size; ECE before and after; the exchangeability assumption and what would break it) and the limitations discussion.

    Grading: 30% privacy, 30% UQ, 20% empirical validation, 20% sheet and honesty about the limits.

    This guarantee sheet is the format required by the trust work package of every Year 2 transverse project ([projects page](../../projects/index.html#trust)).

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

The fiche of this module displays no assessment: its 2026–2027 SynapseS description is not published (see the table of the introduction). Everything below is therefore a proposal: the written exam is a mock final, and the projects are practice that an instructor may adopt as continuous assessment. Every subject exercises objective O8 (trustworthy AI: privacy and uncertainty guarantees) and O7 (hands-on practice: audited pipelines); the graph subjects add O4 and the RAG subject adds O3.

Each project report includes the guarantee sheet of Ex. 11, which is also the format of the trust work package of the Year 2 transverse projects: [Y2.1](../../projects/index.html#y2-1) (conformal abstention), [Y2.2](../../projects/index.html#y2-2) (conformal under shift) and [Y2.5](../../projects/index.html#y2-5) (privacy and calibration of fraud alerts).

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Paper study: an RDP accountant from scratch (Mironov, 2017; Mironov, Talwar and Zhang, 2019).** Question: how much do Rényi DP and subsampling save over advanced composition, and does a short NumPy accountant agree with a production one?
    -   Implement the Gaussian RDP curve, additive composition and the conversion to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ over a grid of orders (Definition 3.3). Then add the RDP of the sampled Gaussian mechanism of Mironov, Talwar and Zhang, a binomial sum for integer orders (ch. 3, 4).
    -   Reproduce Example 3.4, Proposition 4.4 and Ex. 4b. Cross-check against the RDP accountant of Opacus, with the same integer orders, for $q \in \{0.001, 0.01, 0.1\}$ and $\sigma \in \{0.5, 1, 2\}$, up to $10^4$ steps. No data is needed.
    -   Opacus converts RDP to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ with the slightly tighter formula of Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, Hsu and Sato (2020), not with that of Definition 3.3: implement both and report the gap.
    -   Deliverables: code with unit tests, a 4–6 page report with curves of $\varepsilon$ against the number of steps, a 10-minute talk. Success: the RDP curve, and $\varepsilon$ under the same conversion, within 1 % of Opacus on the whole grid; $\varepsilon^* \approx 5.75$ in Example 3.4 with the conversion of Definition 3.3.

2.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Conformal prediction for GNN node classification.** Question: does split conformal keep its 90 % coverage on a citation graph, where the nodes are linked rather than i.i.d.? The subject connects this module to [Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5) and [Advanced GNN](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html).
    -   Train a two-layer GCN (Kipf and Welling, 2017; Graph ML ch. 5) on Cora and PubMed, with the Planetoid splits of PyTorch Geometric. Calibrate on held-out labelled nodes: split conformal with the score of Definition 9.1, then per-class Mondrian conformal (ch. 9).
    -   Compare with naive sets that keep the most probable classes of an MC-dropout average ($S = 50$ passes) or of a 5-GCN ensemble until their mass reaches 90 % (ch. 8). Reproduce the split-conformal baseline of Huang, Jin, Candès and Leskovec (2023).
    -   Break exchangeability on purpose: calibrate on high-degree nodes only, or on one community, and relate the coverage loss to the homophily of the test nodes (ch. 12, "On graphs").
    -   Deliverables: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. Success: mean coverage within one point of 90 % over 50 random calibration/test splits, with the per-class gaps and the shift experiment reported with intervals.

3.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Edge-level versus node-level DP for graph statistics.** Question: what does it cost to protect a person rather than one of their friendships? The subject applies ch. 1–3 to the graph setting of [Advanced GNN 7.4](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch7).
    -   Derive the sensitivities (Definition 1.3) of the edge count, the degree histogram and the triangle count, under edge neighbours and under node neighbours. For node-DP, first project the graph to a maximum degree $D$, and bound how much one node can change the projected graph: this is the subtle step.
    -   Release the statistics with the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms (ch. 2), and an edge-DP top-10 of the highest-degree nodes with the exponential mechanism. Keep the whole budget ledger with RDP composition (ch. 3).
    -   Data: the ego-Facebook and ca-GrQc graphs of SNAP (Leskovec and Krevl, 2014).
    -   Deliverables: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk. Success: curves of relative error for $\varepsilon$ from 0.1 to 10 under both neighbour notions, the gap explained by the ratio of sensitivities, and a justified choice of $D$.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] A private and calibrated readmission model.** Question: can one hospital model be private, calibrated and covered at once, and what does each guarantee cost? The subject extends Ex. 11 to the Diabetes 130-US hospitals data (Strack and coauthors, 2014; UCI repository, about 100,000 encounters).
    -   Member 1: privacy — the privacy unit is the patient, so keep one encounter per patient (about 70,000 rows, as in Strack and coauthors) and row-level DP then protects patients (Definition 1.1). Cohort statistics under a budget $\varepsilon = 1$ with a budget ledger (ch. 1–3); DP-SGD with Opacus for $\varepsilon \in \{1, 3, 8\}$ and $\delta = 10^{-6}$ (ch. 4).
    -   Member 2: attack — a loss-threshold attack and a shadow-model membership inference (ch. 5; [Security & Robustness](../m2-security-robustness/index.html#ch8) Def. 8.3), before and after DP, reported as the true-positive rate at 1 % false positives.
    -   Member 3: uncertainty and decision — temperature scaling and ECE (ch. 7), conformal sets for readmission and CQR intervals for the length of stay (ch. 9–10), a cost-sensitive threshold with abstention to a clinician (ch. 12).
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report, the guarantee sheet of Ex. 11, a 15-minute talk. Success: a privacy–utility–coverage frontier over the three budgets, an attack advantage that shrinks with $\varepsilon$, and coverage within one point of 90 % on held-out patients.

2.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] An abstaining RAG assistant with semantic uncertainty.** Question: can a retrieval-augmented LLM tell when not to answer, with a guarantee on the errors of what it does answer? The subject connects this module to [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch7) ch. 7 and 9, and prepares Y2.1.
    -   Data and models: TriviaQA (Joshi, Choi, Weld and Zettlemoyer, 2017), with its Wikipedia evidence documents as the retrieval corpus. Kuhn, Gal and Farquhar (2023) used the closed-book setting, which is the no-retrieval baseline here. Use an open instruction model of 1–3 B parameters on a free GPU, and an NLI model for entailment, DeBERTa-large fine-tuned on MNLI as in that paper.
    -   Member 1: the RAG pipeline (BM25 and a dense retriever), $K = 10$ sampled answers per question, verbalized confidence (Definition 11.1), correctness by exact match.
    -   Member 2: uncertainty scores — token log-probability, self-consistency and semantic entropy with bidirectional entailment (Definition 11.2); AUROC for correctness and ECE (ch. 7).
    -   Member 3: abstention — a threshold chosen on 500 calibration questions by conformal risk control (Definition 12.2), with the loss "answered and wrong" at $\alpha = 0.1$; the risk–coverage curve; 20 canary strings planted in the document store and an extraction test (ch. 5).
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report with the guarantee sheet, a 15-minute talk. Success: over 20 random calibration/test splits, the mean rate of answered-and-wrong questions stays at or below 10 %; the AUROC of semantic and lexical entropy is reported with intervals, with and without retrieval; canary leakage is measured.

3.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Paper study: conformal fraud alerts under drift on the Elliptic graph (Weber and coauthors, 2019).** Question: does a coverage guarantee survive a regime shift in a transaction graph, and what restores it? The subject prepares Y2.5 and uses the drift monitoring of [MLOps ch. 5](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html#ch5).
    -   Member 1: models — reproduce the temporal split of the paper (train on time steps 1–34, test on 35–49) with a random forest and a GCN (Graph ML ch. 5); calibrate both (ch. 7).
    -   Member 2: guarantees over time — split conformal alert sets calibrated on the last training steps; the coverage per time step through the dark-market shutdown that the paper reports near step 43; recalibration on a rolling window, and Mondrian conformal per class (ch. 9).
    -   Member 3: decisions — a cost-sensitive alert threshold under a budget of analyst reviews per time step, abstention to the analyst, and the risk–coverage curve (ch. 12).
    -   Deliverables: code, a 6–8 page report with the guarantee sheet, a 15-minute talk. Success: the illicit-class F1 of the paper is reproduced within a few points, the coverage drop after the shift is measured, and the report says how much the rolling window recovers and at what cost in set size.

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Format: 2 hours, one handwritten A4 sheet allowed, a non-programmable calculator, four questions. The fiche displays no exam, so this is a mock.

1.  **Question (4 points).** (a) State $\varepsilon$-DP with the neighbour convention of this page, and the post-processing property. Why may a model trained with DP-SGD be published with all its weights? (b) Distinguish aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, and say which of the two the variance between MC-dropout passes estimates. (c) What does the split conformal guarantee promise, and what does it not promise? Give one deployment in which it fails.

    *Expected*: (a) Definition 1.1 with add/remove neighbours, and Proposition 1.2(1). The weights are a post-processing of the noised gradients, whose whole sequence is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP by composition and amplification (ch. 3–4). (b) Definition 6.1; the variance between passes is the epistemic part (Result 8.2).

    (c) Marginal coverage of at least $1 - \alpha$, on average over the calibration draw and the new point (Theorem 9.2). It promises nothing per group or per input. It fails without exchangeability: calibration in one hospital and deployment in another, or after a drift.

2.  **Question (5 points).** (a) A counting query is released with the Laplace mechanism at $\varepsilon = 0.5$. Give the noise scale and the probability of an error of at least 4. (b) A Gaussian counting query is released 100 times with $\sigma = 10\,\Delta_2$. With $\delta = 10^{-5}$, compute the RDP account and its optimal order. (c) An $\varepsilon = 2$ mechanism runs on a Poisson subsample with $q = 0.02$. What is its guarantee?

    *Expected*: (a) the scale is $b = 1/\varepsilon = 2$ and $\mathbb P(|Z| \geq 4) = e^{-2} \approx 0.135$ (Theorem 2.1). (b) Each release is $(\alpha, \alpha/200)$-RDP, and the 100 releases compose into $(\alpha, \alpha/2)$-RDP (Definition 3.3). The conversion gives
    $$\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2} + \frac{\ln 10^5}{\alpha - 1},$$
    minimal at $\alpha - 1 = \sqrt{2 \ln 10^5} \approx 4.8$, where $\varepsilon \approx 2.90 + 2.40 = 5.3$; advanced composition would give about 53. (c) By Proposition 4.4, $\varepsilon' = \ln(1 + 0.02\,(e^2 - 1)) \approx 0.12$.

3.  **Question (5 points).** Let the scores $s_1, \dots, s_{n+1}$ be exchangeable with no ties, and let $\hat q$ be the $k$-th smallest of the first $n$, where
    $$k = \lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil \leq n.$$
    (a) Prove that $\mathbb P(s_{n+1} \leq \hat q) = k/(n+1)$. (b) Deduce that the coverage lies between $1 - \alpha$ and $1 - \alpha + 1/(n+1)$. (c) Give $k$ and the coverage when $(n, \alpha) = (19, 0.1)$. What happens with eight calibration points?

    *Expected*: (a) by exchangeability, the rank of $s_{n+1}$ among the $n+1$ scores is uniform on $\{1, \dots, n+1\}$, and the event $\{s_{n+1} \leq \hat q\}$ is "this rank is at most $k$" (Theorem 9.2).

    (b) By definition of the ceiling,
    $$(n+1)(1-\alpha) \;\leq\; k \;<\; (n+1)(1-\alpha) + 1;$$
    divide by $n+1$.

    (c) Then $k = 18$ and the coverage is exactly $18/20 = 0.90$. With eight points, $k = \lceil 8.1 \rceil = 9$ exceeds $n$, and the set is the whole output space (Example 9.3).

4.  **Question (6 points).** A binary model outputs the logits $z = (3, 0)$, for classes 1 and 0, on a group of patients, 70 % of whom have class 1. (a) Compute the announced probability of class 1, and the temperature that calibrates it on this group. (b) Prove that, for calibrated probabilities and costs $c_{\text{FP}}, c_{\text{FN}}$, predicting 1 minimizes the expected cost exactly when
    $$\hat p \;\geq\; \frac{c_{\text{FP}}}{c_{\text{FP}} + c_{\text{FN}}}.$$
    (c) Predicting 1 triggers a costly protocol, with $c_{\text{FP}} = 3$ and $c_{\text{FN}} = 1$. Compare the decisions and expected costs before and after calibration.

    *Expected*: (a) at $T = 1$, $\hat p = 1/(1 + e^{-3}) \approx 0.95$. Calibration asks $1/(1 + e^{-3/T}) = 0.7$, so $T = 3/\ln(7/3) \approx 3.5$ (Procedure 7.5).

    (b) Predicting 1 costs $c_{\text{FP}}(1 - \hat p)$ on average, predicting 0 costs $c_{\text{FN}}\,\hat p$; the first is smaller exactly above the threshold (Definition 12.2).

    (c) The threshold is $3/4$. Before calibration, $0.95 \geq 0.75$: the model treats everyone, at an expected cost of $3 \times 0.3 = 0.9$ per patient. After calibration, $0.7 < 0.75$: it treats no one, at a cost of $1 \times 0.7 = 0.7$. Miscalibration costs 0.2 per patient.

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness of the guarantees | 30 % | every $\varepsilon$, $\delta$ and coverage level follows from a stated result of the chapters, with its assumptions checked: neighbour convention, accountant, exchangeability |
| Empirical validation | 25 % | coverage and calibration measured over repeated splits with intervals; privacy audited by an attack, not only declared |
| Guarantee sheet and limits | 15 % | the sheet of Ex. 11 is complete, and the report says what would break each guarantee |
| Code and reproducibility | 15 % | one script reruns every number of the report from public data with fixed seeds; the privacy ledger is logged |
| Report and talk | 15 % | a clear question, real references, figures that make the point, precise answers to questions |
